newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Red tape dims allure of Philippine mining.
newsitem.headline: Red tape dims allure of Philippine mining.

text.p: The Philippines continues to offer some of the most exciting mining opportunities in Asia but foreign firms are getting fed up with delays in the approval of new exploration permits, industry executives said on Thursday.

"Bureaucratic delays are frustrating. They result in permits not being approved, exploration not proceeding, and opportunities in the Philippines decreasing," said Malcolm Norris, chairman of the International Mining and Exploration Committee (IMEC).
"Morale in the industry is weakening at a time when more and more opportunities are opening worldwide," he said at a Philippine mining conference attended by government and industry officials.
IMEC groups 34 foreign firms which have applied for exploration permits in the country.

"It costs a lot of money to keep a team here in the Philippines. You cannot keep going back to your parent company when you're being held up...they will look somewhere else to invest," said Tony Robbins, managing director of Australia-based Indophil Resources.
Norris said some IMEC members had applied for permits to the Philippine Mines and Geosciences Bureau eight months ago.
"In other countries like Australia, mining exploration permits are either approved or rejected one or two months after submitting your application," he told reporters.
Foreign firms flocked to the Philippines in 1995 after it liberalised ownership in local mining projects.
But Manila has so far approved only two applications for foreign technical assistance agreements (FTAA) since the Philippine Mining Act was approved.

Norris said between 20 and 25 foreign companies had applied for half of the more than 100 pending applications to explore areas covering four million hectares, or 14 percent of the Philippine land surface.
IMEC members alone are ready to spend $120 million for mining exploration in the Philippines within 12 months after approval of their permits, he said.

"The recognised endowment and poor exploration history (of the Philippines) suggest significant undiscovered potential, that is why most of us are here," Norris, who is also country manager of WMC Exploration Corp, a unit of Australia-based WMC Ltd, said.
Philippine Environment Secretary Victor Ramos said his department hoped to issue 11 more FTAA permits by the end of the year.
"We hope to finish revenue-sharing negotiations with 11 new FTAA applications by year end," he said.

Government and industry officials said FTAA applications were stalled after tonnes of mine waste from Marcopper Mining Corp's copper mine leaked into a nearby river in the central Philippines in March 1996.
The incident sparked protests from environmentalists and indigenous tribes, forcing the government to amend rules of the Philippine Mining Act last December.
Under the new rules, mining firms are required to obtain permission from indigeneous people before exploring ancestral lands and to give them one percent of output as royalty.

The firms are also required to contribute at least one percent of their mining and milling costs every year to community development projects and to set up post-operational land management plans for pits, waste, dams, and tailings structures.
